questions.q: What is described as the single most important Kafka metric to watch?
options: Consumer lag — the gap between the latest offset written and what a consumer group has actually committed
The Kafka version number currently installed
The number of producers connected at any given time
The number of topics in the cluster
questions.explain: Climbing lag directly means a consumer is falling behind the rate events are arriving — the clearest sign real-time processing is breaking down.

questions.q: What does an under-replicated partition indicate?
options: The consumer group has too many members
The topic has been deleted
The partition has too many replicas and needs fewer
One or more replicas has fallen behind or is unreachable, thinning the safety margin replication is supposed to provide
questions.explain: It's an early-warning signal that precedes a real outage, not necessarily an outage itself, tying directly back to Lesson 11's replication coverage.

questions.q: Why does broker disk usage matter as an ongoing concern rather than a one-time decision?
options: Disk usage only matters for consumers, never for brokers
Kafka automatically deletes all data every hour regardless of settings
Retention deliberately holds data for a configured window, so disk usage keeps accumulating as long as that window is active
Disk usage is irrelevant once a broker is first provisioned
questions.explain: Because retention (Lesson 13) keeps data around for a set period, disk usage is a continuous concern tied to that setting, not a one-time sizing exercise.

questions.q: How does consumer lag compare to the watermark/late-data concepts from Fabric & Real-Time Analytics, per this lesson?
options: Watermarks replace the need for consumer lag entirely
Both answer the same underlying question — how far behind is processing relative to when things actually happened — just with different vocabulary
Consumer lag only applies to batch processing, not streaming
They are completely unrelated concepts with no similarity
questions.explain: Kafka expresses this as an offset or time gap; Fabric expresses it against event time and a watermark threshold — same underlying concern, different vocabulary.
